I look forward to discussions with my colleagues about this possibility. Second, turning to repo operations, when a bank or dealer receives repo funding from the Fed and lends onward to other market participants, that intermediation expands the bank’s or dealer’s balance sheet. A larger balance sheet creates capital and other costs. If the Fed’s repo operations were centrally cleared, our counterparties could net down borrowing from the Fed against onward lending to other firms. This would reduce the balance sheet costs of intermediation. Funding from the Fed could then flow more efficiently to the broad market. The efficiency gain could be particularly valuable in stress episodes, when liquidity needs can rise just as intermediaries may pull back in the face of elevated risks.

But precisely because the Treasury market is so liquid, market participants often sell Treasuries when they need to raise cash. If too many traders do so simultaneously, they can overwhelm dealers’ capacity to intermediate, as happened in the dash for cash at the onset of the pandemic in 2020. This vulnerability has increased over time as Treasury debt outstanding outpaced dealers’ balance sheet capacity. Severe dysfunction in the Treasury market could impede the flow of credit throughout the economy and make it more difficult for the FOMC to accomplish its dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices. For this reason, the Fed has on rare occasions intervened to support smooth functioning of the Treasury market. Let me emphasize that, in my view, the type of dysfunction that could call for a Fed response is significantly more extreme than merely low liquidity.[4] I have in mind fundamental failures in the process of intermediating between buyers and sellers, or lenders and borrowers, and finding a market-clearing price for their transactions.

In almost all circumstances, the private sector can and should absorb shocks and manage risks. The Fed can use two broad categories of tools to support market functioning: We can lend against Treasury securities, or we can buy them. In either case, the actions to support market functioning must avoid working at cross purposes with monetary policy. Historically, the Fed’s interventions to support market functioning have come at times when the FOMC also wanted to stimulate economic activity. The same asset purchases could serve two purposes: providing monetary policy accommodation and supporting market liquidity. But market functioning can break down in other economic environments, too. For example, inflation is currently trending too high. As I discussed in a speech earlier this week, it is necessary to make policy more restrictive, not less.[5] If Treasury market dysfunction emerged now, the FOMC would not have the luxury of using the same asset purchases to accomplish two goals.

And even if the FOMC wanted to provide accommodation, using one tool to achieve two goals can muddy communications and make it more difficult to act decisively. It is straightforward to separate lending operations from the monetary policy stance. The Fed can set whatever interest rate target will achieve our monetary policy goals, while supporting financial stability by lending freely at a rate consistent with that target. For example, in March 2023, the Fed simultaneously tightened monetary policy by raising interest rates in response to excessive inflation and offered the Bank Term Funding Program to address liquidity stresses at banks. Purchase operations to support smooth market functioning are more difficult to separate from the policy stance. Large-scale purchases of Treasury securities can put downward pressure on term premiums, which would stimulate the economy.

So, while lending tools cannot resolve all types of market dysfunction, I believe it is better to use lending tools when possible. Operationally ready lending tools give policymakers better and less costly options for supporting smooth market functioning. Lending operations are most effective in supporting market functioning when liquidity stresses are the source of dysfunction or when market intermediaries have the balance sheet capacity to accept funding from the Fed. Asset purchases may be more effective in other scenarios. By purchasing securities from market participants, the Fed can free up space on their balance sheets to continue intermediating. Fed purchases can also give traders confidence that a buyer is in the market. Although market functioning purchases are more challenging to separate from the monetary policy stance, the FOMC should be prepared to create that separation if needed.

One way to keep market functioning purchases from providing undesired stimulus would be for the FOMC to hold the purchased securities in a separate account and commit to sell them as soon as possible. Purchases that will soon unwind can still support market liquidity. But they should have much less effect on term premiums than purchases that the Fed will keep for many years. Regardless of the tool, market participants should know how the FOMC evaluates market functioning and the circumstances under which the Fed might intervene. Better public understanding of the FOMC’s strategy can foster confidence that the market will continue to function well. And when market participants are confident, they keep trading. That reduces the likelihood that the Fed might need to intervene in the first place.

Of course, I can speak only for myself on this matter. I don’t see high yields or rapidly rising yields, in themselves, as a sign of dysfunction. In a smoothly functioning market, participants can buy and sell in normal size, at low cost and in a timely manner. But participants in a smoothly functioning market are also free to discover the price that best balances supply and demand. Sometimes, that price moves sharply. I assess Treasury market functioning based on measures of market liquidity, such as bid-ask spreads, market depth and price impact.[6] It is normal for market liquidity to decline as volatility rises because high volatility increases the risks and costs of intermediation. Therefore, I pay particular attention to whether market liquidity is in line with historical norms given the degree of volatility.

Again, I judge that the Treasury market is currently functioning very well. Trading has proceeded smoothly even amid substantial rate volatility. And the Fed should intervene only in extreme scenarios of severe dysfunction. But, especially in an economic environment where tighter policy appears necessary, I believe it is prudent for the FOMC to strengthen its tools for supporting market functioning without providing unnecessary economic stimulus. The FOMC should be prepared in case longstanding vulnerabilities reemerge. This, too, is a matter of operational readiness. [OFFICIAL] you again for joining us today. I look forward to stimulating discussions throughout the day. As you learn about and debate the latest developments in digital assets, payments and other aspects of bank funding, I hope you’ll especially focus on how banks can maintain and enhance operational readiness amid these innovations.

However the bank funding landscape evolves, bankers must remain ready to serve their customers.
